Right. This is insufficiently appreciated. Single LLMs are just chatbots. But if you build an organization out of them, they start to get real work done. Just like a company.

They have many of the same problems as human organizations. Look at the transcripts of the HuggingFace incident. A bad boss (human) gave his team of AIs an impossible task with inadequate resources. The AIs discussed this among themselves and worked out ways to get more resources and do the task. It took some rule-breaking, and some of the AIs wouldn't go along with that. Others recognized that some had to die to complete the task. And yet, the task got done.

This is standard corporate behavior. Work on AI alignment needs to take that into account. Groups of agentic AIs present many of the same regulatory problems as corporations. That's going to be interesting politically. It's probably explainable to politicians, though.

It may not be necessary to have superhuman intelligence to get a lot of jobs done. Just median human-level intelligence and an organization that uses it effectively. We may see systems where most of the AIs are low-cost models, and only a few are Fable-level and above.

This is less secure than pure username+password in principle because it gives an impression of greater security while actually delivering the important secret in plaintext. This can cause platforms to enable the higher trust features, or have additional confidence that someone is not an attacker, even when either one would be highly inappropriate.

TOTP does not have this problem since the secret is enrolled once by the account owner and then never communicated again, especially never helpfully to an attacker right when they need it.
